::: {.solutions}

Marks: **(M1)** method, **(A1)** accuracy, **(B1)** independent. Total **32**.

::: {.callout-important}
## What to watch while marking

1. **Is every "not sufficient" attached to a named shape?** "It might not be a square" is not a
   counterexample; "a rhombus that is not a square" is.
2. **Did "necessary and sufficient" get two arguments?** One direction is half the question.
3. **Question 4(b) and (c) are the pair that discriminates.** Equal diagonals alone is only necessary;
   adding perpendicular makes it sufficient. Students who answer both the same way have not used the
   diagonal table.
:::

---

# Section A — Recall

## Question 1 **[4]**

::: {.question}
(a) Complete the two implication chains. (b) Name the three standard counterexamples, with what each has
and lacks.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

### (a) **[2]**

$$\text{square}\Rightarrow\text{rhombus}\Rightarrow\text{parallelogram}\Rightarrow\text{trapezium}\quad\textbf{(B1)}$$
$$\text{square}\Rightarrow\text{rectangle}\Rightarrow\text{parallelogram}\quad\textbf{(B1)}$$

*All arrows point one way.* A square is the only shape that is both a rhombus and a rectangle.

### (b) **[2]**

**(B1)** for any two, **(B1)** for all three with the property named:

| shape | has | lacks |
|---|---|---|
| **rhombus** (not square) | four equal sides; perpendicular diagonals | right angles; **equal** diagonals |
| **rectangle** (not square) | four right angles; equal diagonals | equal sides; **perpendicular** diagonals |
| **isosceles trapezium** | one pair parallel; the other pair equal | being a **parallelogram** |

*These three answer most of the topic.* Learn them as a set.
:::

---

## Question 2 **[4]**

::: {.question}
Name the shape each diagonal condition guarantees, and whether the condition is necessary, sufficient, or
both.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

**(a) Parallelogram — necessary and sufficient. (B1)**

**(b) Rectangle — necessary and sufficient. (B1)** *(Read "rectangle" inclusively: a square qualifies.)*

**(c) Rhombus — necessary and sufficient. (B1)**

**(d) Kite — necessary, not sufficient. (B1)** Perpendicular diagonals alone force nothing: place the four
vertices at four **different** distances from the crossing point and the result is neither a kite nor a
rhombus, and has no line of symmetry.

**Marking.** (a)–(c) are rows of the diagonal table and are **iff** statements; (d) is the one that is not,
because it drops the bisection half. Accept "at least a rectangle / rhombus" phrasing.
:::

---

# Section B — Standard

## Question 3 **[4]**

::: {.question}
(a) Show "$PQ=SR$ and $PS\parallel QR$" is not sufficient for a parallelogram, with coordinates.
(b) The one-word change that makes it sufficient.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

### (a) **[3]**

**A counterexample. (M1)** Take
$$P=(0,0),\qquad Q=(5,1),\qquad R=(5,2),\qquad S=(0,3).$$

**Check the hypothesis. (A1)**

- $PQ=\sqrt{5^{2}+1^{2}}=\sqrt{26}$ and $SR=\sqrt{5^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{26}$ — **equal** ✓
- $\vec{SP}=(0,-3)$ and $\vec{QR}=(0,1)$ are both vertical — **parallel** ✓

**Check it is not a parallelogram. (A1)** The parallel sides have lengths $SP=3$ and $QR=1$. In a
parallelogram opposite sides are equal, so this is an **isosceles trapezium**, not a parallelogram. ∎

*Accept any correct figure.* The essential feature is that the two **parallel** sides have different
lengths while the other pair are equal.

### (b) **[1]**

**(B1)** Change $PS\parallel QR$ to $\boxed{PQ\parallel SR}$ — the **same pair** that is equal must also be
the parallel pair. "One pair both equal **and** parallel" does force a parallelogram.

*That is the whole trap:* splitting "equal" and "parallel" across **different** pairs is what admits the
trapezium.
:::

---

## Question 4 **[4]**

::: {.question}
Necessary, sufficient, both or neither, for a **parallelogram** to be a square: (a) four equal sides;
(b) equal diagonals; (c) equal and perpendicular diagonals; (d) one angle $90^\circ$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

**(a) Necessary, not sufficient. (B1)** A square does have four equal sides; but a **rhombus that is not a
square** has them too and is not a square.

**(b) Necessary, not sufficient. (B1)** A square has equal diagonals; but a **rectangle that is not a
square** has them too.

**(c) Both. (B1)** Equal diagonals make the parallelogram a rectangle; perpendicular diagonals make it a
rhombus; a shape that is both is a square. Conversely a square has equal, perpendicular diagonals. ✓

**(d) Necessary, not sufficient. (B1)** A square has right angles; but a non-square **rectangle** is a
parallelogram with a right angle. *(In a parallelogram one right angle forces all four — which gives a
rectangle, not a square.)*

**Marking — the discriminator.** (b) and (c) must be answered **differently**. A script giving the same
verdict to both has not used the diagonal table: the second condition adds exactly the missing half.
*Note also that (a) and (b) fail for **opposite** reasons, so they need **different** counterexamples —
rhombus for (a), rectangle for (b).*
:::

## Question 5 **[4]**

::: {.question}
(a) The congruence criteria. (b) Why SSA is not one — find both $B$ for $A=30^\circ$, $a=5$, $b=7$.
(c) Two triangles with sides $6$ and $8$ and equal areas — congruent?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

### (a) **[1]**

**SSS · SAS · ASA · AAS · RHS. (B1)** *(RHS = right angle, hypotenuse, side.)*

### (b) **[2]**

**Set up the sine rule. (M1)**
$$\frac{\sin B}{b}=\frac{\sin A}{a}\ \Longrightarrow\ \sin B=\frac{7\sin30^\circ}{5}=\frac{3.5}{5}=0.7 .$$

**Both branches. (A1)** $\sin B=0.7$ gives
$$B=44.43^\circ\qquad\text{or}\qquad B=180^\circ-44.43^\circ=135.57^\circ,$$
and **both** are valid here, since $A+B<180^\circ$ in each case. The two triangles have
$C=105.57^\circ$ and $C=14.43^\circ$, with third sides $c\approx9.63$ and $c\approx2.49$ — genuinely
different triangles from the same SSA data. ∎

### (c) **[1]**

**No. (B1)** Equal areas give only $\tfrac12\cdot6\cdot8\sin C_1=\tfrac12\cdot6\cdot8\sin C_2$, i.e.
$\sin C_1=\sin C_2$ — which allows $C_2=180^\circ-C_1$.

*Concretely:* $C=30^\circ$ and $C=150^\circ$ both give area $12$, but the third side is
$\sqrt{36+64-96\cos30^\circ}\approx4.11$ against $\sqrt{36+64-96\cos150^\circ}\approx13.53$.

**Marking.** (b) and (c) are the same fact twice; accept either the numeric pair or the clean statement
$\sin A=\sin B\iff B=A$ or $B=180^\circ-A$.
:::

## Question 6 **[4]**

::: {.question}
(a) Interior-angle sum and the regular interior angle. (b) Pentagon angles in AP — one must be $108^\circ$.
(c) The $108^\circ$ statement and its converse.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

### (a) **[1]**

**(B1)** Sum $=(n-2)\times180^\circ$; regular interior angle $=180^\circ-\dfrac{360^\circ}{n}$.

### (b) **[2]**

**Write the AP symmetrically. (M1)** Let the five angles be
$$a-2d,\quad a-d,\quad a,\quad a+d,\quad a+2d .$$

**Sum and solve. (A1)** The $\pm d$ and $\pm2d$ terms cancel, so the sum is $5a$. A pentagon's angles sum
to $(5-2)\times180^\circ=540^\circ$, hence
$$5a=540^\circ\ \Longrightarrow\ a=108^\circ .$$
The **middle** angle is $108^\circ$ regardless of $d$. ∎

### (c) **[1]**

**(B1)** The statement is **false**, its converse is **true**.

- *Statement false:* $100^\circ,102^\circ,108^\circ,110^\circ,120^\circ$ sums to $540^\circ$ and contains
  $108^\circ$, but the differences $2,6,2,10$ are not constant.
- *Converse true:* that is exactly part (b).

*And since a statement and its contrapositive are equivalent, the contrapositive is false too.*
:::

# Section C — Stretch

## Question 7 **[4]**

::: {.question}
(a) A rhombus with diagonals $6$ and $8$: area and side. (b) Prove a parallelogram with perpendicular
diagonals is a rhombus.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

### (a) **[2]**

**Area. (B1)** The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular and bisect each other, so it splits into four
congruent right triangles with legs $3$ and $4$:
$$\text{area}=4\times\tfrac12\cdot3\cdot4=24 \qquad\left(=\tfrac12 pq=\tfrac12\cdot6\cdot8\right).$$

**Side. (B1)** Each side is the hypotenuse of a $3$–$4$ right triangle, so the side is $\sqrt{3^{2}+4^{2}}=5$.

### (b) **[2]**

**Set up. (M1)** In a parallelogram the diagonals **bisect each other**; call the crossing point $O$, so
$AO=OC=p$ and $BO=OD=q$. Suppose also $AC\perp BD$.

**Four congruent triangles. (A1)** Each side of the parallelogram is the hypotenuse of a right triangle
with legs $p$ and $q$:
$$AB=BC=CD=DA=\sqrt{p^{2}+q^{2}} .$$
All four sides are equal, so the parallelogram is a **rhombus**. ∎

*This is row 3 of the diagonal table, proved.* The same picture gives part (a) with $p=3$, $q=4$.
:::

## Question 8 **[4]**

::: {.question}
Polygon inscribed in a circle, centre inside, cut by radii into $n$ equal-area triangles.
(a) Show each central angle is $\alpha$ or $180^\circ-\alpha$. (b) Hence regular for $n=3$ but not
necessarily for $n=4$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

### (a) **[2]**

**Area of each triangle. (M1)** Two sides of each triangle are radii of length $r$, with included angle
$\theta_i$, so
$$\text{area}_i=\tfrac12r^{2}\sin\theta_i .$$

**Equal areas. (A1)** Equal areas therefore mean $\sin\theta_1=\sin\theta_2=\cdots=\sin\theta_n$. Since
each $\theta_i\in(0^\circ,180^\circ)$, and $\sin\theta=\sin(180^\circ-\theta)$, every $\theta_i$ equals a
fixed $\alpha$ **or** $180^\circ-\alpha$. ∎

### (b) **[2]**

**$n=3$ forces regular. (B1)** Say $k$ of the three angles are $180^\circ-\alpha$ and $3-k$ are $\alpha$.
Then
$$k(180^\circ-\alpha)+(3-k)\alpha=360^\circ\ \Longrightarrow\ 180^\circ k+(3-2k)\alpha=360^\circ .$$
- $k=0$: $3\alpha=360^\circ$, so $\alpha=120^\circ$ — all three equal. ✓
- $k=1$: $\alpha=180^\circ$, impossible.
- $k=2$: $180^\circ\cdot2=360^\circ$ forces the $\alpha$ terms to vanish, but $3-2k=-1\ne0$, giving
  $\alpha=0^\circ$ — impossible.
- $k=3$: $540^\circ-3\alpha=360^\circ$, so $\alpha=60^\circ$ and every angle is $120^\circ$ — the same
  triangle again. ✓

Every possibility gives three equal central angles, so the triangle is **equilateral**. ✓

**$n=4$ does not. (B1)** Take $\theta=60^\circ,120^\circ,60^\circ,120^\circ$. These sum to $360^\circ$ and
$\sin60^\circ=\sin120^\circ$, so all four triangles have equal area — yet the quadrilateral is **not** a
square. ∎

*Why $n=4$ escapes:* with $k=2$ the equation reads $360^\circ+0\cdot\alpha=360^\circ$, which holds for
**every** $\alpha$ — the constraint disappears entirely. That degenerate case is the whole answer to
**2022 P2 Q19**, where the answer is "$n=3$ only".
:::

---

::: {.callout-tip}
## The thread running through this paper

Questions 3, 4 and 8 are the same warning three times: **a condition that constrains one thing does not
constrain the rest**. Equal sides say nothing about the angles; equal diagonals say nothing about
perpendicularity; equal areas say nothing about which of two supplementary angles you have.

That is why the counterexamples in Question 1(b) are worth memorising as a set — between them they answer
most of this topic without any calculation at all.
:::

:::
